## Where We Are {.smaller}

You now understand how computers work at the hardware level: RAM, disk storage, and the cost of accessing data.

. . .

Today: the **file system**, how your computer organizes everything you store.

::: {.notes}
Frame this as the bridge from concepts (Ch 1) to practical skills (Ch 3+). Without understanding file systems, the command line will feel arbitrary and confusing. With this foundation, everything clicks. "Where is my file?" becomes answerable.
:::

---

## What Is a File? {.smaller}

At the fundamental level, everything on your computer is **binary data**: ones and zeros.

. . .

A **file** is a named collection of this binary data stored on disk.

. . .

What makes files useful is **interpretation**: the same bytes mean different things depending on format.

::: {.notes}
Show the concept: the byte sequence for "Hello" looks the same whether a text editor interprets it as text, a hex editor shows it as bytes, or an image viewer sees gibberish. The file itself is dumb; the program reading it decides what it means.
:::

---

## Text vs. Binary Files {.smaller}

| | Text Files | Binary Files |
|---|---|---|
| **Human-readable** | ✅ Yes (characters) | ❌ No (encoded data) |
| **Editable in text editor** | ✅ Yes | ❌ Gibberish |
| **Size efficient** | ❌ Larger | ✅ Compressed |
| **Git-friendly** | ✅ Line-by-line tracking | ❌ Entire file changes |
| **Examples** | .txt, .csv, .py, .md | .xlsx, .jpg, .pdf, .db |

::: {.notes}
This distinction is foundational. When students struggle with file formats later, loop back to this. "Why can't I open this Excel file in Git?" Because it's binary. "What should I use instead?" CSV or JSON (both text). This one table explains 80% of file format decisions.
:::

---

## Common Data Formats {.smaller}

**CSV**: Plain text, rows and columns separated by commas.

```{.text filename="sales.csv"}
date,region,product,revenue
2024-01-15,North,Widget,2999.00
2024-01-16,South,Gadget,4999.50
```

**JSON**: Structured text with nesting, clear data types.

```{.json filename="config.json"}
{"project": "analysis", "year": 2024, "active": true}
```

**YAML/TOML**: Configuration files, human-friendly.

```{.yaml filename="config.yaml"}
project: analysis
year: 2024
active: true
```

**Excel**: Binary archive (ZIP) of XML files, complex but ubiquitous.

::: {.notes}
Demo: Open each of these in a text editor (except Excel). Show how CSV and JSON and YAML are all readable. Excel becomes an opaque blob. When should you prefer each? CSV for data exchange (widest compatibility), JSON for configuration and APIs, YAML for human-written configs, Excel only when your audience demands it.
:::

---

## Why File Formats Matter {.smaller}

Two datasets, identical content, different formats:

- **data.csv**: 2 MB, text-based, Git tracks changes line-by-line
- **data.xlsx**: 500 KB, binary, Git stores entire new copy each time

. . .

For collaboration and version control, **text beats binary every time**.

::: {.notes}
This is a value statement that will guide their project decisions for the rest of the course. Make it stick. "When in doubt, choose text format." They'll hit Excel in the real world (Chapter 20), but by then they'll understand the cost.
:::

---

## The File System Tree {.smaller}

Files live in **directories** (folders). Directories nest inside each other, forming a tree:

```
/                          (root)
├── Users/
│   └── ozan/
│       ├── Documents/
│       │   └── report.md
│       └── Projects/
│           └── sales-analysis/
│               ├── data/
│               │   ├── raw/
│               │   └── processed/
│               └── scripts/
```

Every file has a location. Every location can be specified by a **path**.

::: {.notes}
Draw or display this tree carefully. This mental model is crucial. Students will refer back to it when confused about paths. "Where am I?" becomes answerable by following the branches.
:::

---

## Absolute Paths {.smaller}

An **absolute path** starts from the root and specifies the complete address.

Works from anywhere, regardless of your current location.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**macOS/Linux**
```
/Users/ozan/Projects/sales-analysis/data/sales.csv
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Windows**
```
C:\Users\ozan\Projects\sales-analysis\data\sales.csv
```
:::

::::

Start at root → follow path → arrive at file.

::: {.notes}
Point out path separators differ by OS (forward slash vs backslash). This will matter when students write code. For now, just awareness.
:::

---

## Relative Paths {.smaller}

A **relative path** specifies a location *from where you are now*.

Shorter, more portable, but only work from a specific starting point.

If you're in `/Users/ozan/Projects/sales-analysis`:

```
data/sales.csv
```

This relative path refers to `/Users/ozan/Projects/sales-analysis/data/sales.csv`.

::: {.notes}
Relative paths are the professional standard for shared projects. If you hardcode absolute paths with your username, your code breaks for teammates. Next chapter (CLI) will make this concrete through practice.
:::

---

## Path Symbols {.smaller}

| Symbol | Meaning | Example |
|--------|---------|---------|
| `.` | Current directory | `./script.py` |
| `..` | Parent (up one level) | `../data/` |
| `~` | Home directory | `~/Documents/` |

These symbols save typing and make paths portable.

. . .

```
../../shared/reference.csv
```

Go up two levels, then down into shared, then into reference.csv.

::: {.notes}
LIVE DEMO: Open a file manager. Show the tree. Point to a file and trace the path. Show how `..` moves you up. Click to navigate and show absolute path in address bar. Then show how the relative path is shorter. This is where understanding shifts from abstract to physical.
:::

---

## Hidden Files {.smaller}

Files starting with `.` are **hidden** by default. Hidden files typically store configuration.

Examples you'll encounter:
- `.git/` — Git version control data
- `.gitignore` — Tells Git what to ignore
- `.env` — Environment variables (secrets ⚠️)
- `.venv/` — Python virtual environment

To see them:
- **macOS Finder**: Cmd+Shift+.
- **Windows Explorer**: View → Show → Hidden items
- **Command line**: We'll cover this next chapter

::: {.notes}
Set expectations: hidden files are "hidden for a reason." They're not secret, just out of the way. As they learn Git and Python, these files will become familiar. Emphasize: don't delete a hidden file unless you know what it does.
:::

---

## Project Organization Best Practices {.smaller}

A well-organized project is easier to navigate and collaborate on.

```
my-analysis/
├── README.md              # Project description
├── data/
│   ├── raw/               # Never modify original data
│   └── processed/         # Cleaned versions
├── scripts/               # Python, SQL code
├── outputs/               # Generated reports, figures
└── docs/                  # Additional documentation
```

**Key principle**: Separate raw from processed. Never modify originals. Always reproduce from source.

::: {.notes}
This structure will become the template for their projects all semester. Emphasize the "never modify raw data" principle; it's a professional habit that prevents disasters. When they design their own projects (Chapter 21), they'll build on this foundation.
:::

---

## Prediction Exercise {background-color="#3B4252"}

You're in `/Users/ozan/Projects/sales-analysis/scripts`.

You want to access `/Users/ozan/Projects/sales-analysis/data/raw/sales.csv`.

**What's the relative path?**

. . .

What's the absolute path?

. . .

Which would you use in a collaborative project, and why?

::: {.notes}
Let them work this out. Relative: `../data/raw/sales.csv`. Absolute: `/Users/ozan/Projects/sales-analysis/data/raw/sales.csv`. The key insight: relative paths are portable (work for any teammate), absolute paths break when usernames differ. This is the "why" that makes paths meaningful rather than mechanical.
:::

---

## Path Separators by OS {.smaller}

The character separating directory names differs:

| OS | Separator | Example |
|---|---|---|
| macOS/Linux | Forward slash `/` | `/Users/ozan/file.txt` |
| Windows | Backslash `\` | `C:\Users\ozan\file.txt` |

This difference occasionally causes pain when sharing code.

. . .

Python's `pathlib` module handles this automatically, which is why we'll use it.

::: {.notes}
Foreshadow: when they write Python code to read files (Chapter 14), they'll use `pathlib` which abstracts away this OS difference. For now, awareness is enough. Some students will be on Windows, others on macOS. Code examples will show both where relevant.
:::

---

## Naming Conventions Matter {.smaller}

- **Avoid spaces**: Use hyphens (`my-project`) or underscores (`my_project`)
- **Use lowercase**: Some systems are case-sensitive, others aren't
- **Be consistent**: Pick a style and stick with it
- **Keep it reasonable**: Don't create paths 100 characters long

Good names are self-documenting and easy to type.

::: {.notes}
This seems nitpicky, but bad naming creates friction that compounds. Spaces require escaping on the command line. Inconsistent case causes confusion. Deep nesting becomes hard to navigate. These are habits worth establishing now.
:::

---

## Where We're Headed {.smaller}

You now understand:

- Files are binary data interpreted by format
- Text formats (CSV, JSON) are portable and Git-friendly
- The file system is a tree, navigable via paths
- Paths can be absolute (from root) or relative (from current location)
- Projects should be organized with clear structure

. . .

Next chapter: the **command line** — how to navigate and manipulate this file system by typing commands, not clicking buttons.

::: {.notes}
Recap without reading. Ask: "What's one naming convention you'll adopt for your projects?" or "Why would you choose JSON over Excel?" Then preview: "Next time, you'll navigate this entire tree using only the keyboard. No mouse allowed."
:::

---

## Recap: Key Takeaways {.smaller}

| Concept | Key Point |
|---------|-----------|
| **File** | Binary data + format = interpretation |
| **Text vs. Binary** | Text = readable and Git-friendly, Binary = encoded |
| **Paths** | Absolute (from root), Relative (from here) |
| **Symbols** | `.` (here), `..` (up), `~` (home) |
| **Hidden files** | Start with `.`, store configuration |
| **Organization** | Separate raw from processed, clear structure |

::: {.notes}
Quick reference slide. Don't read it all; just ask if anything needs clarification. Save time for questions.
:::
